We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts (ppm) list: 169.52, 132.43, 130.27, 129.30, 126.70, 126.66, 123.57, 43.30, 26.29.

We need number of methyl (CH3) groups in the molecule. Methyl carbon typically appears around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, but if attached to heteroatoms or carbonyl, shift can be higher (e.g., 30-50). Here we have two aliphatic carbons: 43.30 and 26.29. Likely one is a carbonyl carbon? No carbonyl carbon is around 170 ppm (169.52) which is carbonyl (C=O). So 169.52 is carbonyl carbon (maybe ester, acid, amide). Aromatic carbons are 120-140 region (multiple peaks). So the molecule likely has aromatic ring (6 carbons) plus carbonyl carbon, plus two aliphatic carbons: one at 43.30 (maybe CH2 attached to carbonyl or aromatic) and one at 26.29 (likely CH3). Methyl carbon appears around 20-30 ppm. So there is likely one methyl group.

But need to be sure: Could there be two methyl groups? 43.30 could be a CH3 attached to heteroatom (e.g., O-CH3) which appears around 55 ppm for methoxy. 43 is a bit high for CH3, maybe CH2 next to carbonyl (e.g., CH2-CO). So likely only one methyl.

Thus answer integer 1.

Check if any other data needed? Could also use proton NMR to confirm number of methyl protons. Let's get proton NMR.
